title: Formalizing the classification of finite simple groups in Lean
excerpt: A complete Lean formalization checked every step of the first-generation CFSG proof and uncovered a flaw in the Unbalanced Group Theorem argument.
body:
A recent effort put the entire first-generation proof of the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) into the Lean proof assistant. The proof, which stretches over thousands of journal pages and was assembled by roughly a hundred mathematicians, now lives as a machine-checked development where every inference is verified by Lean’s kernel.

The project not only reproduced the classic result, every finite simple group is either cyclic of prime order, alternating, of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups, but also uncovered a subtle flaw in a published argument for the Unbalanced Group Theorem. The discovery forced the team to replace the faulty step with a new argument that leans on Solomon’s 1976 theory of maximal 2-components.

## Why formalizing CFSG matters

Mathematicians have long treated the classification as a landmark of collaborative proof, yet its sheer length and the variety of sources make it vulnerable to hidden gaps. A formal proof assistant like Lean offers a single source of truth: each lemma, each diagram chase, each case analysis is recorded in a language that the kernel can check for logical consistency.

When the development is complete, the community can query the proof, reuse its components, and build further theory on a rock-solid foundation. The CFSG formalization therefore serves two purposes. First, it provides confidence that the classification truly holds under the strict standards of formal verification. Second, it creates a reusable library of group-theoretic results that can accelerate future formal mathematics.

## The unbalanced group theorem issue

During the translation of the first-generation proof, the team encountered a closure assertion that appeared in a published route to the Unbalanced Group Theorem. The assertion claimed that a certain class of subgroups closed under taking products and intersections, which would allow the theorem to proceed by induction.

When the developers encoded the statement in Lean and attempted to prove it, the system produced counterexamples: concrete finite groups that satisfied the hypotheses but violated the claimed closure. Because Lean forces every step to be explicit, the discrepancy surfaced as a concrete failure rather than a vague “gap” in the narrative.

The source does not provide the exact formulation of the faulty closure, but it notes that the counterexamples were found while formalizing the “first-generation proof.” The discovery prompted the authors to treat the Unbalanced Group Theorem as an open sub-problem within the larger classification effort, rather than assuming the published argument was airtight.

## New argument using Solomon’s maximal 2-components

To rescue the proof, the team turned to a 1976 result of Solomon concerning maximal 2-components. Solomon’s theory describes how a finite group can be built from its 2-local structure, focusing on subgroups that contain a Sylow 2-subgroup and are maximal with respect to that property. The key ingredient in the new argument is Theorem 2.3 from the accompanying paper, which guarantees preservation of simple tops when passing to these maximal components.

In practice, the developers replaced the problematic closure step with a construction that isolates a maximal 2-component, verifies that its simple top satisfies the conditions of the Unbalanced Group Theorem, and then lifts the result back to the original group. The Lean code mirrors the classical reasoning but makes every dependency explicit. The approach sidesteps the need for the disputed closure entirely, and the formal proof now proceeds without any hidden assumptions.

## What the formalization project delivered

Beyond the correction, the project produced a complete, navigable map of the CFSG proof in Lean. The interactive proof map at https://cfsg.axiommath.ai/ lets users hover over each block, paper, book, or article, and see the statements it supplies. The repository on GitHub (https://github.com/AxiomMath/CFSG) contains the Lean source, organized into agents that correspond to the original sources. Contributors include both mathematical and engineering experts, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of large-scale formalization.

The development also generated a set of errata for the literature. The authors are collaborating with group theorists to compile these corrections, and they plan to publish the errata alongside the formal proof. In addition, the project demonstrates that formal methods can handle proofs of unprecedented scale, offering a template for future endeavors in algebra, topology, and beyond.

## The takeaway

Formalizing the classification of finite simple groups not only validates a historic achievement but also reveals hidden issues, such as the faulty closure in the Unbalanced Group Theorem. By replacing the problematic step with an argument based on Solomon’s maximal 2-components, the Lean development restores the proof’s integrity. The result is a machine-checked, reusable library of group theory that can serve as a foundation for further formal mathematics.
